name: Al Hashan (Site A), Libya's first centrifuge site
summary: Libya's first gas-centrifuge research and development site, active 1997-2002 on the outskirts of Tripoli; the pin marks Ain Zara, where an 'Al Hashan Street' is recorded.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I lists it as 'Site A: the original centrifuge R&D location (Al Hashan)'. Paragraphs 22-23: Libya installed a single complete centrifuge there in 2000 and later a larger hall; the equipment was moved to Al Fallah (Site B).
era: Libya moved the equipment to Al Fallah (Site B) by April 2002 and the programme later centred on Al Khalla. The site was declared in 2003-04 and the US, UK and IAEA removed all nuclear equipment by September 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen. No weapons material is reported to remain.
uncertain: The IAEA names the site 'Al Hashan' but gives no suburb, street or coordinates (GOV/2004/12 contains no distances or addresses). The pin is Ain Zara, from GlobalSecurity ('outskirts of Tripoli') and an 'Al Hashan Street' registry address, so it is suburb-level. A 1982 Libyan grain-silo plan also lists an 'al-Hashshan silo' (JPRS 2655), which is probably unrelated.

name: Al Khalla (Site C), centrifuge and conversion site
summary: Suburb-level pin for Libya's second centrifuge site, which succeeded Al Hashan and stored uranium hexafluoride; uranium-conversion modules were assembled here in 1998.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site C: the original site for the Uranium Conversion Facility (Al Khalla)'. Paragraph 17: the conversion modules were stored around Tripoli until 1998, partly assembled at Sawani (Site G), then moved to Al Khalla; paragraph 18: later moved to Salah Eddin (Site D).
era: The conversion modules were later moved on to Salah Eddin. The site was cleared in 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: Suburb-level only. 'Khalla' is the name of a group of neighbourhoods in Salah al-Din (Khalla al-Ferjan, Khalla Bin Oun, with an 'Al Khalla Road' on OpenStreetMap); the sources do not say which one. Pinned at Khalla al-Ferjan with a 2.5 km radius.

name: Salah Eddin (Site D), uranium conversion facility
summary: Suburb of Tripoli where Libya moved its Japanese-supplied uranium conversion facility; IAEA inspectors first saw the modules here in December 2003.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site D: the new site for the UCF (Salah Eddin)'. Paragraph 18: the conversion facility was moved there; the milling and waste-treatment modules stayed at Sawani (Site G).
era: The equipment was verified in 2004 and removed by September 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: Suburb-level only: Salah Eddin is a Tripoli district (also on the map as Salah al-Din) and no source gives a street address. The pin is placed slightly apart from the district marker with a 2.5 km radius.

name: Al Fallah (Site B), second centrifuge site
summary: Where Libya moved its centrifuge equipment by April 2002 and stored uranium hexafluoride; GlobalSecurity suggests it may be the Fallah industrial zone in Tripoli.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site B: the new location for centrifuge R&D, also used to store UF6 (Al Fallah)'; paragraph 23: the equipment moved there from Al Hashan.
era: The site was not publicly tied to Libya's weapons programme until a May 2004 IAEA report.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: GlobalSecurity calls the location 'obscure' and says only that it 'may be the Fallah Industrial Zone, near Markaz Azahif Alakhdar in Tripoli'. The pin is the Fallah area on the Tripoli ring road side with a 2 km radius; treat it as a lead.

name: Al Karamia (Site H), first conversion-module store
summary: Name-match pin for the first storage place of Libya's uranium conversion modules; GlobalSecurity could not find the name in any gazetteer.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site H: the storage location for construction material (Al Karamia)'.
era: Cleared with the rest of the programme in 2004.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: Weakest placement of the group. GlobalSecurity says neither NIMA nor Google had heard of 'Al Karamia'. The pin is the Krimiya (Al-Kirimiya, الكريمية) suburb south-west of Tripoli, chosen only because the name is close; it could be wrong. 3 km radius.

name: El Ezeizia (Site K), construction-materials store
summary: Name-match pin for the original storage site of materials for the Libyan uranium conversion plant; probably the town of Al Aziziyah, south-west of Tripoli.
history: IAEA GOV/2004/12 Annex I: 'Site K: the original construction materials storage location (Al Ezeizia)'. Annex II also lists an 'Al Ezeizia storage site' and an 'Al Ezeizia artillery refurbishment site' among places inspected for weapons capability. A 1980 CIA imagery report says Libya's first Scuds were seen in July 1976 at the 'Al Aziziyah Ammunition Storage Depot'.
today: Not described in the pages seen.
uncertain: The IAEA gives no coordinates. The Aziziyah match is now better supported: the Annex II entries (storage and artillery refurbishment) and the CIA's 'Al Aziziyah Ammunition Storage Depot' are both military stores at Al Aziziyah, and the CIA says SA-5 missiles at 'Al Azizyah' protected Rabta. The depot's exact position is still unpublished, so the pin stays on the town centre with a 3 km radius. Do not confuse it with Bab al-Aziziya in Tripoli.

name: First Scud launch of the 2011 war (about 80 km east of Sirte)
summary: Where Gaddafi's forces fired their first Scud missile on 16 August 2011, reported as about 80 km east of Sirte; it landed in the desert east of Brega.
history: Al Jazeera reported the missile was fired from a location about 80 km east of Sirte and came down east of Brega without injuring anyone. A second Scud was reported fired on 22 August 2011 from near Sirte.
era: NATO strikes reportedly destroyed the remaining Scuds, and by 2011 the Scud-B force was effectively ended.
uncertain: Position is computed from a news distance ('about 80 km east of Sirte') and other reports say only 'from Sirte' or 'near Sirte', so the pin carries a 30 km radius. It marks a launch point, not a base.

name: Bin Ghashir tactical missile (Scud and FROG) facility
summary: A probable tactical surface-to-surface missile base south of Tripoli where US imagery analysts counted at least 21 Scud launchers in 1982. This is the only Scud garrison with published coordinates.
history: A 1982 NPIC briefing board gives the coordinates 32°45′30″N 13°12′30″E and reports elements of at least two Scud brigades and one FROG-7 battalion there for the first time: at least 21 Scud MAZ-543 launchers, five resupply semitrailers, two probable FROG-7 launchers and eight FROG-7 resupply vehicles. It suggests the Scuds may have come from the Kulliyat garrison about 6 nautical miles to the north. A December 1980 NPIC report counted at least 59 Scud launchers in six brigades of 9-10 each, deployed or stored at three facilities in the Tripoli area (Tajura South barracks, Madaniyah barracks, and a barracks and vehicle storage depot) and one at Benghazi, with the first Scuds seen at the Al Aziziyah ammunition depot in 1976.
era: Reported 1980-82; whether the base was still used in 2011 is not established.
today: Not described in the documents used.
uncertain: Coordinates are from the CIA briefing board as transcribed in the archive; the page's own distance line ('… nm south of Tripoli') is garbled. This is not the Bab Ben Ghashir district or the Qasr bin Ghashir town, which are on the map separately. The December 1980 report names the other Tripoli-area Scud sites but gives no coordinates for them in the text we hold.

name: Jarmah missile launch site (OTRAG), later used for Libyan missile development
summary: The German OTRAG rocket range in the Libyan desert, about 380 nautical miles south of Tripoli. By December 1983 CIA imagery said the Libyans were using it to develop a short-range missile.
history: A March 1981 NPIC report describes a fenced site about 2 by 1 km with a 19 m lattice launch tower, propellant storage, 16 prefabricated housing units, workshops, a water reservoir and a 2,370 m runway, built by the West German firm OTRAG after its Zaire range was cancelled in 1979. An August 1982 board records a new concrete launch pad at coordinates 26°33′05″N 13°09′50″E. OTRAG ended its Libyan launch work in December 1981 and left in 1981-82 (Aviation Week; Der Spiegel). A December 1983 board shows a launch in preparation with a crane over the erector-launcher and says the site was 'currently being used by the Libyans for the development of a short-range missile'.
era: 1980-1983; later use is not documented in the sources held.
today: Not described in the documents used.
uncertain: Coordinates are from the CIA briefing boards of 1982 and 1983. Their text says the site is '5.5 nm east of Jarmah', which does not fit the town of Jarma (Germa) on modern maps, so the coordinates are used and the place name is not. Wikipedia places OTRAG's Libyan centre at Tawiwa near Sabha (26.99°N 14.46°E), and GlobalSecurity says a March 1981 test came 'from either the Sebha Oasis or the Jarmah Oasis'; the CIA imagery supports the Jarmah site. Which later Libyan missile programme used it is not stated.

name: Tarabulus Military Storage Area Southeast (first confirmed Scud-B launcher)
summary: Where US imagery analysts first confirmed a Scud-B launcher in Libya, in April 1977, at a military storage area south-east of Tripoli.
history: A top-secret NPIC imagery information report of 21 April 1977 says the first confirmed Scud-B transporter-erector-launcher in Libya was identified at the 'Tarabulus Military Storage Area Southeast', at 32°49′45″N 13°20′26″E. It adds that four probable Scud-B launchers and nine resupply transporters had been seen in July 1976 at the Al Aziziyah ammunition storage depot.
era: 1976-1977; the later organisation of the Scud brigades is covered in the 1980 NPIC report.
uncertain: Coordinates are exact in the report, but the report names the area only as a military storage area and does not say how long Scuds stayed there. Later Scud brigades were at other sites such as Bin Ghashir.
